chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: After thanking Anna Pavlovna for her delightful evening, the guests began to leave.

Pierre was an awkward man. Heavyset, about average height, broad-shouldered, with enormous red hands, he had no idea — as people say — how to enter a drawing room and even less how to exit one gracefully. He was also hopelessly absent-minded. When he stood to go, he picked up the general's three-cornered hat instead of his own and stood there tugging at its plume until the general asked for it back. All of this clumsiness was redeemed, however, by his kind, simple, and genuinely modest expression. Anna Pavlovna turned to him with a Christian gentleness that conveyed forgiveness for his blunders, nodded, and said: "I hope to see you again, but I also hope you'll change your opinions, my dear Monsieur Pierre."

He made no reply and only bowed, but once again everyone noticed that smile of his — a smile that said nothing at all, except perhaps: "Opinions are opinions, but can't you see what a decent, good-natured fellow I am?" And everyone, including Anna Pavlovna, could feel this.

Prince Andrew had gone out into the hall and, with his shoulders turned to the footman helping him on with his cloak, listened with cold indifference to his wife chattering with Prince Hippolyte, who had also come out. Prince Hippolyte stood close to the pretty, pregnant princess, staring at her through his monocle.
[Speaking in French] "Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess, taking leave of Anna Pavlovna. "It's settled," she added in a low voice.
Anna Pavlovna had already managed to speak with Lise about the match she was arranging between Anatole and the little princess's sister-in-law.
"I'm counting on you, my dear," said Anna Pavlovna, also speaking softly. "Write to her and let me know what her father thinks of it. Goodbye!" And she went back inside.
Prince Hippolyte walked up to the little princess and, leaning his face close to hers, began whispering something.

Two footmen — the princess's and his own — stood holding a shawl and a cloak, waiting for the conversation to end. They listened to the French being spoken, which meant nothing to them, with an expression that suggested they understood perfectly well but were too polite to show it. The princess, as always, spoke with a smile and listened with a laugh.
"I'm so glad I didn't go to the ambassador's," said Prince Hippolyte. "So dull. It's been a delightful evening, hasn't it? Delightful!"
"They say the ball will be wonderful," the princess replied, drawing up her soft little lip. "All the prettiest women in society will be there."

"Not all — because you won't be there. Not all," said Prince Hippolyte with a joyful smile. And snatching the shawl from the footman — even pushing the man aside — he began wrapping it around the princess. Whether from clumsiness or by design (no one could tell which), after adjusting the shawl he kept his arm around her for a long time, as though embracing her.
Still smiling, she moved gracefully away, turning to glance at her husband. Prince Andrew's eyes were closed — he looked utterly weary and sleepy.
"Ready?" he asked his wife, looking past her.

Prince Hippolyte hurriedly threw on his cloak, which in the latest fashion reached all the way to his heels, and stumbling in it, ran out to the porch after the princess, whom a footman was helping into the carriage.
[Speaking in French] "Princess, goodbye!" he cried, stumbling over his words as much as his feet.
The princess, gathering up her skirt, was taking her seat in the dark carriage. Her husband was adjusting his saber. Prince Hippolyte, under the pretense of helping, was getting in everyone's way.
"Step aside, sir," said Prince Andrew in Russian, his tone cold and unpleasant, to Prince Hippolyte who was blocking his path.
"I'm expecting you, Pierre," said the same voice, but now gentle and affectionate.
The driver started and the carriage wheels clattered. Prince Hippolyte stood in the porch laughing convulsively as he waited for the vicomte, whom he had promised to take home.

[Speaking in French] "Well, my friend," said the vicomte, settling himself beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming, very charming indeed — quite French." And he kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing.
"You know, for all your innocent airs you're quite the rascal," the vicomte continued. "I pity the poor husband — that little officer who puts on the airs of a king."
Hippolyte spluttered with laughter again. "And you were saying Russian ladies can't compare with the French? You just have to know how to handle them."

Pierre arrived at the house first and went into Prince Andrew's study as if he owned the place. Out of habit he immediately flopped down on the sofa, grabbed the first book his hand found on the shelf — it happened to be Caesar's Commentaries — and, propping himself on his elbow, began reading from the middle.
"What have you done to Mademoiselle Scherer? She's going to be quite ill after that," said Prince Andrew as he came into the study, rubbing his small white hands.
Pierre rolled his whole body over, making the sofa creak. He turned his eager face toward Prince Andrew, smiled, and waved his hand.
"That abbé is very interesting, but he's got it all wrong. In my opinion, perpetual peace is possible, but — how do I put it — not through a balance of political power..."
It was obvious that Prince Andrew had no interest in this kind of abstract discussion.
"You can't go around saying everything you think, my friend. Anyway, have you finally decided on anything? Are you going to be a guardsman or a diplomat?" asked Prince Andrew after a brief silence.
Pierre sat up on the sofa with his legs tucked under him.
"Honestly, I still don't know. I don't like either option."
"But you have to choose something! Your father expects it."

Pierre had been sent abroad at the age of ten with a tutor — an abbé — and had stayed away until he was twenty. When he returned to Moscow, his father dismissed the tutor and told the young man: "Now go to Petersburg, look around, and choose a career. I'll agree to anything. Here's a letter to Prince Vasili, and here's money. Write and tell me everything, and I'll help you however I can." Pierre had been trying to choose a career for three months now and had settled on nothing. It was this choice that Prince Andrew was asking about. Pierre rubbed his forehead.
"But he must be a Freemason," he said, referring to the abbé he had met that evening.
"That's all nonsense," Prince Andrew interrupted again. "Let's talk about something real. Have you been to the Horse Guards?"

"No, I haven't. But here's what I've been thinking, and I wanted to tell you: there's a war on against Napoleon. If it were a war for freedom, I'd understand it and I'd be the first to enlist. But to help England and Austria against the greatest man in the world — that's not right."

Prince Andrew merely shrugged at Pierre's naive words. He put on the look of a man who finds it pointless to reply to such nonsense, though in truth it would have been hard to give any better answer than the one he gave to this simplistic question.
"If nobody fought except from personal conviction, there would be no wars," he said.
"And that would be wonderful," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew smiled with irony.
"Very likely it would be wonderful, but it will never happen."
"Well then, why are you going to war?" asked Pierre.
"Why? I don't know. I have to. Besides, I'm going..." He paused. "I'm going because the life I'm leading here doesn't suit me!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: The rustle of a woman's dress was heard from the next room. Prince Andrew gave a start as if waking from sleep, and his face took on the expression it had worn in Anna Pavlovna's drawing room. Pierre swung his feet off the sofa. The princess came in. She had changed into a house dress that was just as fresh and elegant as the one before. Prince Andrew stood and politely pulled out a chair for her.

[Speaking in French] "How is it," she began, settling quickly and fussily into the armchair as she always did, "how is it that Annette never got married? How foolish you men all are for not marrying her! Forgive me for saying so, but you have no understanding of women whatsoever. What a debater you are, Monsieur Pierre!"

"And I'm still arguing with your husband. I can't understand why he wants to go to war," replied Pierre, speaking to the princess without any of the awkwardness young men usually show around young women.
The princess flinched. Pierre's words had clearly struck a nerve.

"That's exactly what I tell him!" she said. "I don't understand it at all — I simply cannot understand why men can't live without wars. How is it that we women want nothing of the kind, have no need for it? You be the judge between us. I'm always telling him: here he is, Uncle's aide-de-camp, the most brilliant position. Everyone knows him, everyone thinks so highly of him. Just the other day at the Apraksins' I heard a lady ask, 'Is that the famous Prince Andrew?' I really did!" She laughed. "He's received so well everywhere. He could easily become aide-de-camp to the Emperor himself. The Emperor spoke to him so graciously, you know. Annette and I were just discussing how to arrange it. What do you think?"
Pierre glanced at his friend and, seeing that he disliked the conversation, said nothing.
"When do you leave?" he asked.

"Oh, don't talk about his going — don't! I won't hear a word about it," said the princess in the same petulant, playful tone she had used with Hippolyte in the drawing room — a tone that was clearly out of place in this intimate family setting of which Pierre was practically a member. "Today, when I remembered that all these wonderful connections will have to be broken off... and then, you know, André..." She looked pointedly at her husband. "I'm frightened — I'm so frightened!" she whispered, and a shudder ran through her.
Her husband looked at her as though surprised to discover that someone besides Pierre and himself was in the room, and spoke to her with icy politeness.
"What exactly are you afraid of, Lise? I don't understand," he said.
"There — that's just like men! All of you — all egotists! Just on some whim of his own, God knows why, he abandons me and locks me away in the country all alone."
"With my father and sister, don't forget," said Prince Andrew gently.
"Alone all the same — without any of my friends. And he expects me not to be afraid."

Her voice had turned querulous now, and her lip was drawn up, giving her face not a joyful expression but an animal one — like a squirrel's. She paused, as if it would be improper to mention her pregnancy in front of Pierre, though that was the heart of the matter.
"I still can't understand what you're afraid of," said Prince Andrew slowly, his eyes fixed on his wife.
The princess blushed and threw up her arms in a gesture of despair.
"No, Andrew, I have to say it — you've changed. Oh, how you've changed..."
"Your doctor says you should go to bed earlier," said Prince Andrew. "You should go."
The princess said nothing, but suddenly her soft downy lip began to tremble. Prince Andrew stood up, shrugged his shoulders, and paced the room.
Pierre looked over his glasses with naive bewilderment — first at one, then at the other. He half rose as if to leave but then thought better of it.

"Why should I mind Monsieur Pierre being here?" the little princess exclaimed suddenly, her pretty face all at once crumpling into a tearful grimace. "I've wanted to ask you for so long, Andrew — why have you changed toward me? What have I done? You're going off to war and you have no pity for me. Why?"
"Lise!" was all Prince Andrew said. But that single word contained a plea, a warning, and above all the certainty that she herself would regret what she was saying. She rushed on regardless:
"You treat me like an invalid — or a child. I can see it perfectly well! Is this how you behaved six months ago?"
"Lise, I'm asking you to stop," said Prince Andrew, more firmly now.
Pierre, who had grown more and more distressed listening to all of this, stood up and went over to the princess. He seemed unable to bear the sight of tears and was on the verge of crying himself.

"Please calm yourself, Princess! It only seems that way because... I assure you, I've felt the same... because... No, forgive me! I'm an outsider — I have no business here. No, please don't upset yourself... Goodbye!"
Prince Andrew caught him by the hand.
"No, wait, Pierre! The princess is too kind to want to deprive me of the pleasure of spending the evening with you."
"No — he only thinks of himself," the princess muttered, unable to hold back her angry tears.
"Lise!" said Prince Andrew dryly, raising his voice to that pitch which signals that patience has run out.

Suddenly the angry, squirrel-like expression on the princess's pretty face transformed into a look of winning, pitiful fear. Her beautiful eyes darted sideways toward her husband's face, and her expression became timid and pleading — like a dog that rapidly but weakly wags its drooping tail.
[Speaking in French] "My God, my God!" she murmured, and gathering up her skirt with one hand, she went to her husband and kissed him on the forehead.
"Good night, Lise," he said, rising and kissing her hand with the formal courtesy he might have shown a stranger.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: The two friends sat in silence. Neither wanted to be the first to speak. Pierre kept glancing at Prince Andrew; Prince Andrew rubbed his forehead with his small hand.
"Let's go have supper," he said with a sigh, moving toward the door.

They went into the elegant, newly decorated dining room, where everything was luxurious. From the table napkins to the silver, china, and glassware, everything bore that look of newness you find in the homes of the recently married. Halfway through supper, Prince Andrew leaned his elbows on the table with an expression of nervous agitation that Pierre had never seen on his face before, and began to speak — like a man who has been carrying something inside him for a long time and has suddenly decided to let it out.

"Never, never get married, my friend! That's my advice: don't marry until you can say to yourself that you've done everything you're capable of, and until you've stopped loving the woman you've chosen and can see her exactly as she is — or you'll make a terrible, irreversible mistake. Marry when you're old and good for nothing — otherwise everything that's good and noble in you will be lost. It'll all be wasted on trivialities. Yes! Yes! Yes! Don't look at me with such surprise. If you marry while you still expect something from yourself, you'll feel at every turn that for you it's all over, all finished — except for the drawing room, where you'll stand in a row alongside a court lackey and a fool! But what's the use of talking about it..." He waved his arm.
Pierre took off his glasses, which made his face look quite different, his good-natured expression even more apparent, and stared at his friend in astonishment.

"My wife," Prince Andrew went on, "is an excellent woman — one of those rare women around whom a man's honor is safe. But, my God, what wouldn't I give to be unmarried right now! You're the first and only person I've said this to, because I'm fond of you."

As he said this, Prince Andrew was nothing like the Bolkonski who had lounged in Anna Pavlovna's armchairs, murmuring French phrases through half-closed eyes. Every muscle of his thin face was quivering with agitation; his eyes, in which the spark of life had seemed completely extinguished, now blazed with a brilliant light. It was clear that the more lifeless he appeared in ordinary company, the more passionate he became in these moments of almost feverish intensity.

"You don't understand why I'm saying this," he continued, "but it's the whole story of a life. You talk about Bonaparte and his career" — though Pierre had not mentioned Bonaparte — "but when Bonaparte was working toward his goals, he moved forward step by step. He was free. He had nothing to think about except his aim, and he achieved it. But tie yourself to a woman and, like a prisoner in chains, you lose all freedom! And whatever hope and strength you have just weighs you down and fills you with regret. Drawing rooms, gossip, balls, vanity, triviality — that's the enchanted circle I can't break out of. I'm going to war now, the greatest war there has ever been, and I know nothing and I'm fit for nothing. I'm perfectly charming and I have a sharp wit," Prince Andrew continued, "and at Anna Pavlovna's everyone hangs on my words. And that mindless circle that my wife can't live without, and those women... If you only knew what society women are really like — what women in general are really like! My father is right. Selfish, vain, stupid, shallow in every way — that's what women are when you see them as they truly are! When you meet them in society, you think there's something there, but there's nothing — nothing — nothing! No, don't get married, my friend. Don't marry!" Prince Andrew concluded.
"It's strange to hear you say that," said Pierre. "You — you think you're incapable and your life is ruined? You have everything ahead of you, everything. And you..."
He didn't finish the sentence, but his tone made clear how highly he regarded his friend and how much he expected from his future.

"How can he talk like that?" Pierre wondered. He considered his friend a model of perfection because Prince Andrew possessed in the highest degree precisely those qualities Pierre himself lacked — qualities that could best be described as strength of will. Pierre was continually amazed by Prince Andrew's calm way of dealing with everyone, his extraordinary memory, his immense learning — he had read everything, knew everything, and had an opinion about everything — but above all by his capacity for work and study. And if Pierre was sometimes struck by Andrew's lack of talent for philosophical reflection — something Pierre was particularly drawn to — he saw even this not as a flaw but as a sign of strength.
Even in the best, most friendly, and simplest relationships, praise and encouragement are essential — just as grease is necessary to keep wheels turning smoothly.
"My part is played out," said Prince Andrew. "There's no point talking about me. Let's talk about you," he added after a pause, smiling at his own reassuring thoughts.
That smile was instantly reflected on Pierre's face.

"But what is there to say about me?" said Pierre, his expression relaxing into a carefree, cheerful grin. "What am I? An illegitimate son!" He suddenly turned bright red, and it was obvious this confession had cost him great effort. "No name and no fortune... And really..." But he didn't say what "really" was. "For now I'm free and doing all right. Only I haven't the faintest idea what to do with myself. I wanted to ask your advice seriously."
Prince Andrew looked at him warmly, yet even in that friendly, affectionate glance there was a consciousness of his own superiority.

"I'm fond of you, especially because you're the one truly alive person in our whole circle. Yes, you're doing fine! Choose whatever you want — it's all the same. You'll be fine anywhere. But listen: stop seeing the Kuragins and living that kind of life. It's so wrong for you — all that wild living, all that excess!"
"What can I say, my friend?" Pierre answered with a shrug. "Women, my friend — women!"
"I don't understand it," said Prince Andrew. "Women who are respectable — that's a different matter. But the Kuragin circle, 'women and wine' — I just don't understand it!"
Pierre was living at Prince Vasili Kuragin's house and sharing in the debauched lifestyle of his son Anatole — the very son they were planning to reform by marrying him off to Prince Andrew's sister.

"You know what?" said Pierre, as if suddenly struck by a brilliant idea. "Seriously, I've been thinking about this for a long time. Living the way I do, I can't make decisions properly — I can't think clearly about anything. My head aches and I spend all my money. He asked me to come tonight, but I'm not going."
"You give me your word of honor?"
"On my honor!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: It was past one in the morning when Pierre left his friend's house. It was a cloudless northern summer night. Pierre hailed an open cab, intending to drive straight home. But the closer he got to his house, the more impossible it seemed to go to sleep on a night like this. It was bright enough to see far down the empty street, and it felt more like dawn or dusk than the middle of the night. On the way, Pierre remembered that Anatole Kuragin was expecting the usual crowd for cards that evening, after which there would typically be a drinking session, ending with the kind of amusements Pierre was particularly fond of.
"I should go to Kuragin's," he thought.

But he immediately remembered his promise to Prince Andrew not to go. Then, as happens with people of weak character, he wanted so desperately to enjoy those familiar pleasures one more time that he decided to go anyway. The thought immediately came to him that his promise to Prince Andrew didn't really count, because he had already promised Prince Anatole he would come before he gave Andrew his word. "Besides," he told himself, "all these 'words of honor' are just social conventions with no real meaning — especially when you consider that you could be dead by tomorrow, or something so extraordinary might happen that honor and dishonor become equally meaningless!" Pierre often talked himself out of his own decisions with reasoning like this. He went to Kuragin's.

When he reached the large house near the Horse Guards barracks where Anatole lived, Pierre walked through the lit entrance, climbed the stairs, and went in through the open door. There was no one in the front hall; empty bottles, cloaks, and boots were scattered around; there was a smell of alcohol, and from somewhere deeper in the house came shouting and the sound of voices.

Cards and supper were over, but the guests had not yet left. Pierre tossed off his cloak and entered the first room, where the remains of supper lay on the table. A footman, thinking no one was watching, was secretly finishing off what was left in the glasses. From a third room came bursts of laughter, the shouting of familiar voices, the growling of a bear, and general chaos. About eight or nine young men were crowded anxiously around an open window. Three others were roughhousing with a young bear — one pulling it by its chain, trying to set it on the others.
"A hundred on Stevens!" shouted one.
"No holding on!" cried another.
"I'm betting on Dolokhov!" yelled a third. "Kuragin, separate their hands!"
"Leave the bear alone — there's a bet to settle!"
"One go — or he loses!" shouted a fourth.

"Jacob, bring a bottle!" shouted the host — a tall, handsome young man standing in the middle of the group, coatless, his fine linen shirt unbuttoned at the chest. "Hold on, boys — here's Petya! Good man!" he called out, turning to Pierre.

From the window, another voice rang out — a man of medium height with clear blue eyes, his tone strikingly sober among all the drunken shouting: "Come here — settle the bets!" This was Dolokhov, an officer of the Semenov regiment, a notorious gambler and duelist who was living with Anatole. Pierre smiled and looked around cheerfully.
"I don't understand. What's going on?"
"Wait — he hasn't had enough to drink yet! A bottle here," said Anatole, and snatching a glass from the table, he went over to Pierre.
"First things first — you have to drink!"

Pierre drained one glass after another, peering from under his brows at the rowdy guests who had crowded back around the window, and listening to their chatter. Anatole kept refilling Pierre's glass while explaining that Dolokhov had made a bet with Stevens, an English naval officer, that he could drink an entire bottle of rum while sitting on the outer ledge of the third-floor window with his legs dangling over the edge.
"Come on, drink it all," said Anatole, handing Pierre the last glass, "or I won't let you go!"
"No, that's enough," said Pierre, pushing Anatole aside, and he walked up to the window.
Dolokhov was gripping the Englishman's hand and repeating the terms of the bet clearly and precisely, addressing himself mainly to Anatole and Pierre.

Dolokhov was of medium height, with curly hair and light blue eyes. He was about twenty-five. Like all infantry officers, he wore no mustache, so his mouth — the most striking feature of his face — was clearly visible. The lines of that mouth were remarkably well defined. The middle of his upper lip formed a sharp point and pressed firmly against the lower one, and something like two separate smiles played constantly around the corners; combined with the bold, insolent intelligence in his eyes, this created a face impossible to overlook. Dolokhov was a man without money or connections. Yet despite the fact that Anatole spent tens of thousands of rubles, Dolokhov lived with him and had established himself so firmly that everyone who knew them — including Anatole himself — respected Dolokhov more than they respected Anatole. He could play any card game and nearly always won. No matter how much he drank, he never lost his composure. Both Kuragin and Dolokhov were at that time notorious among the wild set of Petersburg.

The bottle of rum was brought. Two footmen, clearly rattled by the shouting and orders of the young gentlemen, were working to force out the window frame that prevented anyone from sitting on the outer sill.
Anatole strutted up to the window with his usual swagger. He wanted to smash something. Shoving the footmen aside, he grabbed the frame and tugged, but couldn't budge it. He smashed a pane of glass.
"You have a go, Hercules," he said, turning to Pierre.
Pierre grabbed the crossbeam, pulled hard, and ripped the oak frame out with a crash.
"Take it all the way out, or they'll think I'm holding on," said Dolokhov.
"Is the Englishman backing out? Hm? Are we ready?" said Anatole.
"All set," said Pierre, watching Dolokhov approach the window with the bottle of rum in his hand. Through the opening, the light of the sky was visible — dawn blending into the last glow of sunset.
Dolokhov jumped onto the windowsill, the bottle still in his hand. "Listen!" he called out, standing there and addressing the room. Everyone fell silent.

"I bet fifty imperials" — he spoke in French so the Englishman could understand, though his French wasn't very good — "I bet fifty imperials... or would you prefer to make it a hundred?" he added, turning to the Englishman.
"No, fifty," the Englishman replied.

"Fine. Fifty imperials that I will drink an entire bottle of rum without taking it from my mouth, sitting out there on that ledge" — he leaned down and pointed to the sloping surface outside the window — "with my legs hanging over the edge and without holding on to anything. Agreed?"
"Agreed," said the Englishman.
Anatole turned to the Englishman and, grasping one of his coat buttons and looking down at him — the Englishman was short — began repeating the terms of the wager in English.

"Wait!" Dolokhov shouted, banging the bottle on the windowsill to get everyone's attention. "Hold on, Kuragin. Listen! If anyone else does the same thing, I'll pay him a hundred imperials. Understood?"

The Englishman nodded but gave no sign of whether he intended to take up this challenge himself. Anatole wouldn't let go of him, and although the Englishman kept nodding to show he understood, Anatole went on translating Dolokhov's words into English. A thin young fellow — a hussar of the Life Guards who had been losing all evening — climbed onto the windowsill, leaned out, and looked down.
"Oh! Oh! Oh!" he murmured, staring down at the stone pavement.
"Get back!" Dolokhov shouted, shoving him away from the window. The young man stumbled awkwardly back into the room, tripping over his spurs.

Setting the bottle on the windowsill within easy reach, Dolokhov climbed slowly and carefully through the window and lowered his legs. He braced himself against both sides of the frame, settled into position, shifted a little to the right, then to the left, and picked up the bottle. Anatole brought two candles and set them on the sill, though it was already quite light. Dolokhov's back in its white shirt and his curly head were lit from both sides. Everyone crowded to the window — the Englishman in front. Pierre stood there smiling, saying nothing. One man, older than the rest, suddenly pushed forward with a look of alarm and anger and tried to grab Dolokhov's shirt.
"This is madness! He'll be killed!" said this more sensible man.
Anatole stopped him.
"Don't touch him! You'll startle him, and then he really will fall. Eh? What then? Eh?"
Dolokhov turned around and, gripping with both hands again, readjusted himself on his perch.
"If anyone interferes again," he said, squeezing the words out through his thin, compressed lips, "I'll throw him down there myself. Now then!"

With that, he turned back around, let go with his hands, took the bottle, and raised it to his lips. He threw his head back and lifted his free hand for balance. One of the footmen, who had bent down to pick up broken glass, froze in that position, his eyes locked on the window and on Dolokhov's back. Anatole stood rigid, eyes wide. The Englishman watched from the side, lips pursed. The man who had tried to stop it all ran to a corner and threw himself face-down on the sofa. Pierre covered his face with his hands — a faint smile lingering on his features even though his expression now showed nothing but horror and fear. Everyone was completely still. Pierre took his hands away from his eyes. Dolokhov was still sitting in the same position, only his head was thrown further back until his curly hair touched his shirt collar, and the hand holding the bottle rose higher and higher, trembling with the effort. The bottle was visibly emptying, rising higher still, his head tilting back even more. "Why is it taking so long?" thought Pierre. It felt like more than half an hour had passed. Suddenly Dolokhov's spine arched backward and his arm shook convulsively; this was enough to make his whole body start sliding on the sloped ledge. As he began to slip, his head and arm wavered even more with the strain. One hand moved as if to grab the windowsill, then pulled back without touching it. Pierre covered his eyes again and told himself he would never open them. Then suddenly he felt a commotion all around. He looked up: Dolokhov was standing on the windowsill, his face pale but radiant.
"It's empty."
He tossed the bottle to the Englishman, who caught it neatly. Dolokhov jumped back into the room. He reeked of rum.
"Bravo! Well done! Now that's a bet! Unbelievable!" came the shouts from all sides.
The Englishman pulled out his purse and began counting out the money. Dolokhov stood frowning, saying nothing. Pierre leapt up onto the windowsill.
"Who wants to bet me? I'll do the same thing!" he cried suddenly. "Forget the bet — just like that! Someone bring me a bottle! I'll do it! Bring a bottle!"
"Let him try, let him try," said Dolokhov with a smile.
"Are you insane? Absolutely not! No one's letting you do that! You get dizzy just on a staircase!" several voices cried at once.
"I'll drink it! Bring me a bottle of rum!" Pierre yelled, slamming the table with a drunken, determined fist and getting ready to climb out the window.
They grabbed him by the arms, but he was so strong that everyone who touched him went flying.
"No, you'll never manage him like that," said Anatole. "Wait — I'll talk him round. Listen! I'll take your bet tomorrow, but right now we're all going to ——'s."
"Let's go then!" cried Pierre. "Let's go! And we're bringing the bear!"
He grabbed the bear, lifted it in his arms, and began dancing around the room with it.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Prince Vasili kept the promise he had made to Princess Drubetskaya, who had spoken to him on behalf of her only son Boris at Anna Pavlovna's soiree. The matter was brought before the Emperor, an exception was granted, and Boris was transferred into the Semenov Guards regiment with the rank of cornet. He did not, however, receive an appointment to Kutuzov's staff, despite all of Anna Mikhaylovna's efforts and pleading. Shortly after Anna Pavlovna's reception, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to Moscow and went straight to the home of her wealthy relatives, the Rostovs, with whom she always stayed when in town. It was here that her beloved Boris — who had only recently joined a line regiment before being transferred to the Guards as a cornet — had been raised from childhood, living with the family for years at a stretch. The Guards had already departed Petersburg on the tenth of August, and her son, who had stayed behind in Moscow to get his equipment, was to catch up with them on the march to Radzivilov.

It was St. Natalia's day, and also the name day of two members of the Rostov family — the mother and the youngest daughter — both named Nataly. Since early morning, carriages drawn by six horses had been arriving and departing in a steady stream, bringing visitors to the Countess Rostova's grand house on the Povarskaya, which was known to all of Moscow. The countess herself and her beautiful eldest daughter sat in the drawing room receiving the congratulatory visitors, who came and went in an endless succession.

The countess was a woman of about forty-five with a thin, Eastern-looking face, clearly worn out from childbearing — she had borne twelve children. A slowness in her movements and speech, the result of physical exhaustion, gave her a dignified air that commanded respect. Princess Anna Mikhaylovna Drubetskaya, who as a member of the household also sat in the drawing room, helped receive and entertain the guests. The younger members of the family were in the inner rooms, seeing no need to take part in greeting visitors. The count himself met each guest at the door and saw them off, inviting everyone to dinner.

[Speaking in French] "I'm so very grateful to you, my dear" — he called absolutely everyone "my dear," whether they were above or below him in rank, without the slightest change in tone — "I thank you on my own behalf and on behalf of our two dear ones whose name day we're celebrating. But you must come to dinner — I'll be offended if you don't, my dear! On behalf of the whole family, I insist — please come, my dear!" He repeated these words to every single guest without exception or variation, wearing the same expression on his full, cheerful, clean-shaven face, giving the same firm handshake and the same quick, repeated bows. As soon as he had seen one visitor out, he returned to whoever was still in the drawing room, pulled a chair up close, and with his legs spread out comfortably and his hands on his knees — the posture of a man who enjoys life and knows how to live it — he swayed back and forth with easy dignity, made small talk about the weather or asked after someone's health, switching between Russian and very poor but thoroughly confident French. Then, like a man weary but committed to his duties, he would get up to see the next visitor off, smooth his sparse gray hair over his bald spot, and invite them to dinner too. Sometimes, on his way back from the entrance hall, he would pass through the conservatory and pantry into the great marble dining room, where tables were being laid for eighty guests. He would watch the footmen carrying in silver and china, rearranging tables, and unfolding damask tablecloths, and call over Dmitri Vasilyevich — a man of good family who managed all his affairs — and say with evident pleasure at the sight of the enormous table: "Well, Dmitri, make sure everything is just right? Good! The important thing is the service — that's what matters." And with a satisfied sigh, he would head back to the drawing room.

"Marya Lvovna Karagina and her daughter!" the countess's enormous footman announced in his deep bass voice as he entered the drawing room. The countess thought for a moment and took a pinch of snuff from a gold snuffbox decorated with her husband's portrait.

"I'm completely exhausted by all these visitors. Still, I'll see her — but after this, no more. She's so affected. Show her in," she told the footman in a weary voice, as though saying: "Very well, finish me off."
A tall, stout woman with a proud bearing entered the drawing room alongside her round-faced, smiling daughter, their dresses rustling as they came.

"Dear Countess, it's been ages! She's been unwell, the poor thing — at the Razumovski ball — and Countess Apraksina — I was so delighted..." The sounds of lively women's voices tumbled over one another, mingling with the rustling of dresses and the scraping of chairs. And so began one of those conversations that lasts just long enough for the guests to rise at the first pause with a rustle of silk and say: "I'm so delighted... Mamma's health... and Countess Apraksina..." before rustling back out to the entrance hall, putting on cloaks or mantles, and driving away. The conversation turned to the main topic of the day: the illness of the famously wealthy and handsome Count Bezukhov — a celebrated figure from Catherine's era — and his illegitimate son Pierre, the very same young man who had behaved so badly at Anna Pavlovna's reception.
"I feel so sorry for the poor count," said the visitor. "His health is so fragile, and now this trouble with his son — it's enough to kill him!"
"What trouble is that?" asked the countess, as if she didn't already know what the visitor was referring to, though she had heard the story of Count Bezukhov's distress at least fifteen times.

"That's what modern education gets you," declared the visitor. "Apparently, while he was abroad, the young man was allowed to do whatever he pleased. Now in Petersburg, I hear he's been up to such terrible things that the police had to step in."
"You don't say!" said the countess.

"He fell in with bad company," Anna Mikhaylovna cut in. "Prince Vasili's son, and that Dolokhov fellow — from what I hear, the three of them have been up to God knows what. And they've all paid for it. Dolokhov has been demoted to the ranks, and Bezukhov's son was sent back to Moscow. As for Anatole Kuragin — his father managed to hush the whole thing up somehow, but even he was ordered to leave Petersburg."
"But what exactly did they do?" asked the countess.

"They're absolute hooligans, especially Dolokhov," replied the visitor. "He's the son of Marya Ivanovna Dolokhova — such a respectable woman — but just imagine! The three of them got hold of a bear from somewhere, put it in a carriage, and took off to visit some actresses. The police came to intervene, and what did those young men do? They tied a policeman and the bear back to back and threw them both into the Moika Canal! There was the bear, swimming around with the policeman on its back!"
"What a picture that poor policeman must have made, my dear!" the count roared, shaking with laughter.
"Oh, how terrible! How can you laugh about it, Count?"
But the ladies themselves couldn't help laughing.

"They could barely rescue the poor man," the visitor continued. "And to think — this is the son of Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov, amusing himself in this 'intelligent' fashion! And he was supposed to be so well-educated and clever. This is what a foreign education amounts to! I hope that no one in Moscow will receive him, no matter how rich he is. They tried to introduce him to me, but I flatly refused — I have daughters to think of."

"Why do you say he's rich?" asked the countess, turning away from the girls, who immediately put on expressions of elaborate disinterest. "All his children are illegitimate. I believe Pierre is illegitimate too."
The visitor made a dismissive gesture.
"I think there must be a good twenty of them."
Princess Anna Mikhaylovna joined the conversation, clearly wanting to display her connections and her insider knowledge of society.

"The fact of the matter is," she said meaningfully, also lowering her voice, "everyone knows Count Cyril's reputation. He's lost track of how many children he has. But this Pierre was always his favorite."
"How handsome the old man still was, just a year ago!" remarked the countess. "I've never seen a more handsome man."

"He's changed terribly now," said Anna Mikhaylovna. "Well, as I was saying — Prince Vasili is next in line to inherit through his wife, but the count is very fond of Pierre. He looked after his education and even wrote to the Emperor about him. So when he dies — and he's so ill now that it could happen at any moment; Doctor Lorrain has come specially from Petersburg — no one knows who will get his enormous fortune: Pierre or Prince Vasili. Forty thousand serfs and millions of rubles! I know all this firsthand — Prince Vasili told me himself. Besides, Cyril Vladimirovich is my mother's second cousin. He's also Boris's godfather," she added, as if this last detail were of no particular importance.
"Prince Vasili arrived in Moscow yesterday. I hear he's here on some official inspection," the visitor remarked.
"Yes, but between us," said the princess, "that's just a cover story. The real reason is that he's come to see Count Cyril Vladimirovich, having heard how ill he is."

"But you know, my dear, that was a marvelous joke," said the count. Noticing that the older visitor wasn't listening, he turned to the young ladies. "I can just picture the policeman — what a sight he must have been!"

And waving his arms to impersonate the policeman, his portly frame shook once more with deep, resonant laughter — the laughter of a man who always eats well and, especially, drinks well. "So you will come to dinner, won't you?" he said.
